It should encourage deconfliction mechanisms that protect ports, storage facilities, and humanitarian convoys. And it should request regular reporting on secondary impacts in countries far from the conflict but heavily reliant on imports for basic staples. Third, we need coordinated action to build resilient food systems. Member states should expand strategic grain and fertilizer reserves, especially as global markets remain tight and price spikes are increasingly frequent. International financial institutions should scale up shock responsive financing for vulnerable importers facing rising import costs. Regional organizations should strengthen early warning networks for food, energy and transport disruptions. Humanitarian actors need predictable multi-year funding to stabilize markets during crises. And the UN system should integrate food security risk analysis into all peace and security assessments, reflecting the reality that conflict-driven food crises are now systemic, not episodic. It should request technical risk assessments from FAO, WFP, UNCTAD, IMO and UNEP when conflicts threaten global food systems. It should mandate operational briefings on critical choke points, ports, straits, pipelines and fertilizer production hubs whose disruption can push millions into acute food insecurity. And it should encourage the Secretary-General to facilitate agreements on safe maritime passage, de-escalation around critical infrastructure, and humanitarian exemptions for food and fertilizer trade. Global food systems are now frontline casualties of conflict. The Council has the mandate, the tools, and the responsibility to act earlier, more decisively, and with greater coordination. As such, assistance contributes to regional instability and undermines maritime security around the Strait of Hormuz. Madam President, the United States has demonstrated utter disregard for international law. The U.S. maritime blockade of Iran and attacks on Iranian commercial vessels in international waters constitute grave violations of Iran's sovereignty, freedom of navigation, and international law of the sea. U.S. CENTCOM publicly stated on 12 August that U.S. forces had redirected 59 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two. These unlawful measures, alongside the so-called Operation Economic Outcast announced yesterday, 24 August, by the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, are seeking to impose an economic blockade on brave Iranian people, weaponizing food, energy, trade, and access to essential goods as instruments of pressure and warfare. Such unlawful measures cannot be justified under the pretext of security or freedom of navigation. US measures violate fundamental human rights and the principles of sovereign equality, non-intervention, and freedom of navigation, constitute a material breach of Security Council Resolution 2417, and seek to circumvent the functions entrusted to the Security Council under the UN Charter. What is at stake is the integrity of international law. If such unlawful acts are allowed to go unchallenged, it would set a dangerous precedent. The Security Council must categorically condemn and reject these unilateral coercive measures aimed at compelling sovereign states to alter their lawful economic interests and foreign relations. We call on all states to reject and denounce the extraterritorial application of unilateral coercive measures by the United States regime, aimed at compelling member states to subordinate their sovereign rights and lawful policies to those of other states. The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves its right to pursue all available avenue to seek accountability, reparation, and redress, and to hold those responsible to account for the consequences of these unlawful acts. Iran also reaffirms its inherent right of self-defense under international law in the face of the continued U.S. aggressive and unlawful acts. Madam President, Iran's measures are lawful and defensive in nature. As a coastal state to the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has a legitimate right under international law to take necessary measures in response to aggression against its territory and sovereignty. Claims to the contrary have no legal basis. The only sustainable path toward restoring peace, regional stability, and safe maritime navigation is to end aggression. fully respect Iran's sovereignty and territorial integrity, lift unlawful blockade and unilateral coercive measures, and provide credible guarantees against any recurrence of aggression. Any arrangements concerning the Strait of Hormuz can only be established, regulated, and managed by its littoral states, namely Iran and Oman. Madam President, in conclusion, I categorically reject the unfounded allegations made by certain members against Iran regarding alleged disruption to maritime trade and navigation in and around the Strait of Hormuz. rather than addressing the root causes of the current crisis, these allegations deliberately ignore the unlawful aggression against Iran, overlook grave violations of international law, and seek to shift responsibility from the aggressors to the victim. Thank you, Madam President.
Thank the representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Paraguay.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Paraguay thanks Denmark for this opportunity to take the floor. We welcome this high-level debate, whose theme is of particular importance to us. It might seem repetitive, but it is necessary to say this ad nauseam, that we cannot have development without peace or peace without development. And this council has the heavy responsibility of making the security pillar a source of policy that enables development by reestablishing or building peace. necessary to underscore that this body has recognized in the past the direct link between hunger and warfare and has affirmed that food insecurity caused by conflicts constitutes a threat to international peace and security. Madam President, currently both the work of this charter body as well as the fulfillment of the UN's SDGs are are coming up against many difficulties above and beyond the reasons behind this reality, we must improve the efficacy of the system in general, both the peacekeeping architecture as well as the way it works in complementarity with development activities that should be part of the value chain that strengthens the capacities of countries coming outside of internal or international armed conflicts. Food security is a multidimensional issue. It can mean a breakdown in the development process, going back to initial steps or a rupture of the rule of law. In this regard, it can be both a cause as well as a consequence of confrontation and conflict, as we've seen in the many active conflicts that we see around the world, where we have borne witness to the fact that the civilian population is the one that suffers the worst consequences, particularly women and girls. Madam President, we cannot allow entire populations, particularly women and children, to face hunger due to armed conflicts, because the consequences of this reality will always be catastrophic. Preserving human life, therefore, must be an absolute priority. The protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure are the responsibility of all parties to a conflict. and these were included in the obligations set forth in international humanitarian law. At this organisation, we have made very lofty commitments, beginning with ones that we must honour as Charter obligations. Colleagues, peace is not something that can be achieved immediately, but rather a continuous process that can continue to be built, in particular when it comes to dealing with the causes that lead to conflicts. We know that this is a constant concern, the fact that in the framework of an armed conflict, The more harm caused to the civilian population or civilian infrastructure, in particular critical infrastructure of a given country, the more difficult it is to engage in sustainable peace processes. From our country's point of view, this Council could benefit from working more closely with the Resident Coordinator system working on the ground in the same vein, Withdrawal strategies and reintegration of peacekeeping missions must have flexible time frames for withdrawal that enable them to strengthen national institutions and thus facilitate the work of the natural development bodies once the PKO has withdrawn. The World Food Programme has warned about the fact that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz threatens causing an additional 40 pushing an additional 45 million people to acute food insecurity if this conflict continues. And that's why we underscore that we must ensure that the strait is fully reopened and that international maritime law is fully respected. given the consequences around the world, the disruption of global supply chains for food and goods related to agricultural production. Madam President, we conclude by underscoring the fact that implementation of resolution 2417, which was unanimously adopted in this Council, is important and reiterate our support to it. fulfilment of it when it comes to all of the situations of conflict we see around the world. Thank you very much.
Thank you for the statement and I now give the floor to the representative of Kenya.

Thank you Madam President. I thank Denmark for convening this timely debate. I also thank the Secretary General and the other briefers for their valuable contributions. In today's interconnected global economy, food insecurity is no longer confined to the immediate geography of armed conflict. Distant populations continue to be impacted by conflict that trigger cascading shocks through energy markets, fertilizer supply chains, maritime corridors, financial systems, and humanitarian logistics networks miles away. Additionally, the interplay of conflict, climate extremes, displacements, economic pressures, and fragile food systems continue to deepen grievances, hate and vulnerability, and undermine stability. Reports of the 266 million people across 47 countries and territories who face acute food insecurity in 2025 are deeply concerning. They underscore the mutually reinforcing relationship between conflict and food insecurity and the importance of addressing food insecurity as a component of conflict prevention and sustaining peace. Kenya's own experience illustrates these interconnections. In early 2026, approximately 429,000 people in Kenya's refugee settlements face crisis level food insecurity amid reductions in international humanitarian financing. Kenya continues to protect and assist the refugees while addressing its own food security needs, where approximately 3.7 million people in its arid and semi-arid lands were at risk of crisis level or worse food insecurity by June 2026. While this situation was driven primarily by poor and erratic rainfall, global conflict related increases in the cost of food, fuel and agricultural input compounded by the vulnerability of affected communities. Madam President, we believe that the Security Council has an important and distinct responsibility under Resolution 2417. In this regard, we propose for mutual reinforcing priorities. First, we encourage a stronger connection between early warning, early political engagement, and early action supported by integrated analysis of how conflict disrupts food production, markets, livelihoods, humanitarian operations, and access to essential supplies, early warning should be treated as an opportunity for prevention rather than a retrospective description of crisis. Second, we call for continued attention to protect civilians as well as their conditions for and objects indispensable to their survival. Relevant resolutions can be implemented in a manner that safeguards humanitarian access and systems through which people obtain food. Unilateral export restrictions, excessive market speculation and disruptions to the movement of food, fuel and fertilizer must be addressed through coordinated multilateral action. Food, water and agricultural infrastructure must never be targeted or used as instruments of warfare. Third, Kenya urges the international community to invest in food system resilience before crisis occur to enable food systems to absorb shocks and prevent temporary disruptions from escalating into prolonged hunger and instability. Member states supported by international and regional partners should strengthen agricultural production, water management, infrastructure markets, and diversified supply arrangements. Developing countries should be supported to address food insecurity and unlock their full potential through infrastructure, technology transfer, and predictable investment. Fourth, we encourage strengthening the Secretary-General's good office through a more systematic framework that draws on reports. assessments and advice from United Nations system, regional organizations, scientific institutions to link political mediation with technical, humanitarian, and scientific expertise and ensure timely and evidence-based prevention action. Madam President, in conclusion, Kenya underscores clear policy imperative that preventing conflict is also a food security policy. preventing protecting food system is an essential component of peace and security and investing in resilience constitutes a practical form of conflict prevention. I thank you.
Thank you, representative of Kenya for the statement and I now give the floor to the representative of Thailand.

Thank you, Madam President. Thailand would like to commend Denmark for convening this very timely and important debate and We would like to thank all briefers for their insights. The figures that we have heard today are stark, such as the World Food Programme's calculation that 70% of people facing acute food insecurity live in conflict-affected countries. Disruptions have driven up oil and fertilizer prices, placing immense pressure on food security and putting up to 45 million more people at risk of hunger. Therefore, my country would like to highlight three key points. First of all, ensuring access to food during armed conflict is non-negotiable. All parties must uphold and fully comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and show life timely and unimpeded humanitarian access and of course refrain from using starvation as a method of warfare. In line with sustainable development goal two on zero hunger, conflict should not reverse progress toward protecting those in vulnerable situations. Secondly, Strengthening resilient food system is key to withstanding disruptions to global trade and supply chains. Thailand advocates for an open, transparent, predictable and rule-based multilateral trading system that facilitates the uninterrupted flow of food and agricultural inputs, especially during crisis. We must also build resilience by by boosting domestic capacity and promoting precision, smart, and sustainable farming to protect livelihoods, mitigate primary driver of conflict, and contribute to lasting peace. And thirdly, climate action is indispensable to achieving long-term food security as climate change acts as a threat multiplier. Thailand remains firmly committed to achieving net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. And reaffirms that the UNFCCC and its Paris Agreement must remain the cornerstone of global climate governance. We must advance both mitigation and adaptation efforts in accordance with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Indeed, call on developed countries to fulfill their financial commitments to support developing countries climate action. Madam President, there can be no lasting peace without full security and no full security where conflict continues to destroy livelihoods. We must prevent crisis before they escalate and exercise utmost restraint, refrain from the use of force and pursue diplomatic means for the peaceful settlement of disputes. In conclusion, as the world's eighth largest exporter of agricultural and food producers, Thailand remains committed to being a trusted partner in promoting global food security to ensure that food remains accessible to all. Thank you very much for your kind attention.
I thank the representative of Thailand for the statement and I now give the floor to the representative of Belgium.

Madam President, colleagues, Belgium aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union and its Member States and would like to add a few remarks in its national capacity. At a time when conflict is increasingly driving food insecurity, both within and far beyond areas of hostilities, today's debate is particularly timely. We thank the Presidency for convening it, as well as the Secretary General, Acting Executive Director Skar and Dr. Benoit for the clarity of their briefings and recommendations. In too many situations, hunger is no longer merely a consequence of conflict. It is the result of choices made by parties to conflict. Resolution 2417 provides us with a strong framework for action. our responsibility now is to turn its commitments into concrete results. Allow me to highlight three points. First, starvation must simply never be used as a weapon of war. Starvation of civilians is prohibited under international humanitarian law. Attacks on food production and agricultural infrastructure, as well as the deliberate obstruction of humanitarian assistance, have devastating consequences for civilians. The Security Council has a responsibility not only to respond to food crisis, but also to address the conditions that create them and ensure that early warning leads to early action. Upholding international law and accountability must be part of that response. Second, we must better anticipate the wider consequences of conflict on global food security. Conflicts disrupt markets, maritime routes, energy flows, and supply chains. They destroy livelihoods, displace communities, and restrict access to land, water, essential services, and humanitarian corridors. Today's unsown fields become tomorrow's failed harvests. Those already facing food insecurity pay again the highest price. At the same time, climate-related shocks are increasingly compounding conflict-related vulnerabilities. The cost of prevention is invariably lower than the cost of crisis response. This is why Belgium strongly supports anticipatory action, prevention and resilience building. Third, humanitarian and resilience actors need adequate and predictable financing. Belgium remains a principal donor committed to providing a mix of core funding and flexible, predictable, multi-year and needs-based humanitarian funding. We particularly value the role of the Central Emergency Response Fund and other pooled funds, which ensure that resources reach people where needs are greatest and enable humanitarian actors to respond rapidly and efficiently to emerging crises. We thank all donors who continue to support pooled funds and we will continue to advocate for high quality core funding. Madam President, to conclude, hunger in conflict is not inevitable. Too often people starve, not because warning signs were absent, but because protection failed, access was denied and action came too late. Humanitarian assistance alone cannot solve this challenge. We must also address the conflicts, insecurity and structural vulnerabilities that drive food insecurity in the first place. Belgium calls for a principled, preventive and protection-centred response, one that places the dignity and survival of civilians at its core. I thank you.
Thank you for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Ireland.

Madam President, many thanks to Denmark for putting a spotlight on this critical issue. I also thank the Secretary-General and the others for the briefing provided earlier. Ireland aligns with the statements by the European Union and the Group of Friends of Action on Conflict and Hunger, which we co-chair with Sierra Leone. The recent and shameful experience of famine in Gaza and Sudan calls for decisive responses to roll back man-made and conflict-induced starvation. While some contexts have improved, the overall situation, we know, remains profoundly grave. The latest Hunger Hotspots report shows that the populations in Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen, Palestine, Nigeria, and Somalia already face or risk entering catastrophic levels of acute food insecurity. President, we know that conflict remains the leading driver of food insecurity in a context where parties to conflict too often disregard their obligations under international humanitarian law. This is unacceptable. We therefore call on all member states to respect and ensure respect for international humanitarian law. I want to highlight two particular contexts in that regard. In Sudan, Attacks on civilians and the destruction of infrastructure and goods essential for their survival are intensifying, with 14 areas at risk of famine. As a member of the Coalition for Atrocity Prevention and Justice in Sudan, we call on the RSF and SAF to protect civilians, including by ending the use of hunger as a weapon of war. Despite progress, the entire Gaza Strip is still in a crisis level of food insecurity and malnutrition. Aid access has been reduced since February, while economic recovery is held back by restrictions on imports, including of non-jewel use agricultural inputs such as seeds. We call on Israel to remove restrictions on aid access to Gaza in line with its commitments under the peace plan and its obligations under international humanitarian law. We also support EU action in response to Israel's breaches of international law there. Madam President, through our EU Presidency programme, Ireland is facilitating discussions on advancing food security and nutrition, focusing attention on addressing humanitarian needs in Gaza and elsewhere, and backing plans for strengthening the Team Europe approach to humanitarian diplomacy. For our part, Ireland will provide more than EUR 250 million in nutrition intervention and EUR 330 million in humanitarian aid globally this year, while maintaining a strong focus on hunger hotspots. We will continue to partner with organizations, including the UN, the Global Network Against Food Crises, the African Union, and the Global Coalition Against Conflict and Hunger in fighting food insecurity and malnutrition and upholding the right to adequate food. Madam President, I thank you.

I thank the representative of Ireland for the statement and I now give

the floor to the representative of El Salvador.

Thank you very much, Madam President. We thank you for convening this high-level debate and without a doubt, as we've heard throughout today, the issue of food security is very well documented and the relationship between conflict and food security is very well documented. Conflicts continue to worsen access of populations of food, water and livelihoods and also aggravate pre-existing vulnerabilities and prolong their effects beyond the immediate duration of hostilities. These patterns confirm a reality that the council recognized eight years ago now in resolution 2417 in 2018. Hunger related to conflict is not just a humanitarian consequence, but rather a challenge that can have broader implications for international peace and security. For El Salvador, the real challenge now is making progress with existing commitments to move towards more effective implementation. To achieve this, first of all, we must guarantee full respect for international humanitarian law. The use of hunger against civilian populations as a method of warfare is unacceptable. It's therefore necessary to broaden our understanding of the harm caused by conflicts, As the Secretary General has said, the consequences cannot be measured exclusively by the number of victims immediately, but destruction or degradation of agricultural lands, irrigation systems, markets, water networks, energy infrastructure or supply routes can have indirect effects and cumulative effects that can persist for years and seriously compromise the livelihoods of regions, countries and entire communities. Secondly, Madam President, we must strengthen the preventive dimension of resolution 2417. Early warning mechanisms enable us to identify the contexts where food insecurity is quickly getting worse as a result of conflicts. However, how useful these tools are depends on our ability to translate the information available into timely actions. The council should not be reduced to reacting once a situation has reached critical levels. It must use the information provided by the whole of the UN system more systematically and strengthen coordination with humanitarian actors and other specialized actors, particularly when there are clear risks to food security and the livelihoods of civilian populations. And this preventive dimension is all the more relevant when we see the effects that conflicts can have beyond the areas that are directly affected, like disruption to supply chains, to markets, to trade routes or access to essential inputs. Thirdly, El Salvador believes that it's essential to link this discussion to peacebuilding. Our own national experience has taught us that the end of hostilities is an essential condition for peace. However, it is not sufficient to sustain peace. Armed conflict has had a profound impact on rural communities, has caused displacements and had consequences on production, access to land and livelihood. The peacebuilding process required therefore not only political and institutional reforms, but also measures geared towards reintegration, economic recovery and the rebuilding of the communities that were affected. Our experience informs our belief that food security and the recovery of people's livelihoods must be part of a comprehensive vision of prevention and peacebuilding. In this context, Madam President, the PBC has a particularly relevant role. Its ability to bring together the UN system, international financial institutions and other partners to discuss priorities defined nationally can contribute to addressing more coherently the causes and consequences of food insecurity in contexts affected by armed conflict. What's more, the PBC can support international attention beyond the immediate response, promote long-term approaches focused on resilience for communities and facilitating better articulation between prevention, development and peacebuilding. Madam President, the regulatory and normative framework exists and early warning systems are in place. Our challenge is ensuring that our response is not restricted to managing the immediate consequences of crises, but rather that it incorporates a preventive and long term perspective. And for my country, this involves protecting the civilian population during conflicts, acting in a timely manner when we see risks of food insecurity and supporting recovering livelihoods, strengthening resilience and rebuilding communities as a comprehensive part of our efforts to build and to sustain peace. Thank you very much.

Thank you, representative of El Salvador, for the statement. There are still a number of speakers remaining on my list for this meeting.

I intend, with the concurrence of members of the Council, to suspend the meeting until tomorrow at 3:00 p.m.

The meeting is suspended.
